findings.claim: Swapping `util.cachedInternal` for `util.cached` likely changes the property descriptor of the memo cell (`enumerable`/`configurable`), which can cause the lazy `value` getter to be invoked by generic enumeration (spread, `Object.keys`, `JSON.stringify`, structured clone of the internals) instead of only on explicit access.
findings.rationale: The `*Internal` helpers in this file exist precisely to define hidden/non-enumerable lazy members (cf. `util.defineLazyInternal` used two lines below for `propValues`). If `cached` produces an enumerable getter, anything that walks the object will force `normalizeDef(def)` to run eagerly. For object schemas whose `shape` is a lazily-evaluated getter (the `newSh` branch just above), forcing normalization early can evaluate not-yet-defined recursive schemas, producing wrong/partial shapes or infinite recursion. I can't read `util.ts` here, so this is inference from the naming convention and the neighboring `defineLazyInternal` usage — medium confidence, but it is the whole semantic content of this diff and deserves verification.

findings.claim: The cached normalized def is never invalidated when `def.shape` is replaced by the shape setter defined just above, so `_normalized.value` can go stale.
findings.rationale: The block ending at line 2107 installs a getter/setter pair that can swap in a new shape (`newSh`) after construction. Once `_normalized.value` has been read, both `cached` and `cachedInternal` freeze the result, so any later shape mutation is invisible to consumers of `_normalized`. This is pre-existing behavior, but the diff touches exactly this memoization and a change in when the getter first fires (see the other finding) changes how likely the stale value is to be captured — worth a second look while this line is being modified. Medium-low confidence that it is reachable in practice.
